sections.heading: What is the Tree BFS Pattern?
sections.content: Tree BFS (Breadth-First Search) visits a tree level by level, from the root downward and from left to right. It uses a queue: take a node from the front, process it, then add its children to the back. Because the queue always holds the current level followed by the next one, you can count how many nodes belong to the current level and handle each level as a group. It runs in O(n) time and uses O(w) space, where w is the maximum width of the tree.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Traverse a tree level by level (level order traversal)
Find the minimum depth or the shallowest node that meets a condition
Return one value per level (average, maximum, rightmost, leftmost)
Connect nodes on the same level (next pointers)
Zigzag or bottom-up level order
Find the nearest node, the level of a node, or cousins
Compute the width of a tree or check if it is complete
Keywords: level, level by level, depth, minimum depth, right side view, nearest, width, zigzag

sections.heading: TreeNode Definition
The Intuition
sections.content: Imagine dropping a stone into water. The ripples spread outward one ring at a time. BFS works the same way: first the root, then all nodes one step away, then all nodes two steps away, and so on. Since the first time BFS reaches a node is always along the shortest path (fewest edges), BFS is the natural choice for minimum depth and shortest-path questions in unweighted trees and graphs.

The Four Steps Inside Every Level Loop
items: 1. Read queue.size before the inner loop, because the queue changes while you add children
2. Remove exactly that many nodes with removeFirst()
3. Process each node (collect value, compare, link)
4. Add its non-null children to the back of the queue

Put each new level at the front
No node may appear after a null

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Using queue.size inside the loop condition instead of saving it first, which mixes levels
Adding null children to the queue (except in problems that need null markers)
Using DFS recursion for minimum depth and exploring the whole tree
Forgetting that minimum depth ends at a leaf, not at a node with one missing child
Not checking for an empty tree (root == null) before starting
Integer overflow when summing node values or indexing nodes for width (use Long)
Using a List with removeAt(0) as a queue (O(n) per removal); use ArrayDeque
Mixing up addFirst and addLast, which reverses the traversal order

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Tree BFS uses a queue and visits the tree level by level
The level size trick (read queue.size, then process that many nodes) separates levels
BFS is the best fit for minimum depth, nearest node and anything that asks for a level
Time is O(n) and space is O(width of the tree)
Use ArrayDeque for the queue, never removeAt(0) on a list
Only add non-null children, unless the problem needs null markers such as the completeness check
